A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MonoScale and provide readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Corresponding methods, proofs, agent configurations, memory schemas, and case studies can be matched across the appendix renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original GAIA and HLE-MCQ experiments, including agent-pool scaling, malfunctioning-worker evaluations, and execution case studies.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds original ablation, memory-transfer, larger-pool, assumption-validation, cost, and variance results.

M1.justification: The frozen router, agent-conditioned task synthesis, success/failure memory construction, and conservative fallback remain unchanged. v2's practical-instantiation paragraph and Algorithm 1 explicitly document the existing candidate-selection procedure; they do not establish a new algorithm.

E1.justification: Appendix D.2 adds standardized TaskCraft tasks as generic familiarization data for the non-customized warm-up control, extending the onboarding data beyond agent-conditioned synthesis. Evaluation remains on GAIA and HLE-MCQ; the larger pools and different router backbones are configuration changes.

E2.justification: Table 4 adds comparisons against variants without negative memory and without customized warm-up; Table 5 compares native and transferred memories. The original benchmark baseline roster remains. UniRoute, StageRoute, and EvoRoute receive discussion, but full implementations are not reported as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New designs include controlled component removal, direct Qwen-to-Gemini-3-Flash memory transfer, HLE expansion to 20 workers by adding ten Gemini-2.5-Pro-based agents, archived-plan replay on 100 HLE questions, and a 40-task GAIA variance subset. Tables 1 and 3 also redefine relative gains against same-count no-memory controls rather than the three-agent starting point. The original main evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's malfunctioning-pool evaluation and case studies, v2 adds checks of non-interference and fallback compliance, component ablations, memory-transfer analysis, scaling beyond ten agents, and onboarding-cost analysis. Appendix D.7 additionally investigates the existing six-agent accuracy dip and attributes failures to tool-budget exhaustion.

E5.justification: v2 adds a limited uncertainty audit absent from v1: three independent seeds on 40 GAIA tasks, with accuracy standard deviations of 2.89, 1.44, and 2.89 percentage points at five, seven, and ten agents. Appendix C.2 also calls the 19/100 versus 21/100 replay difference nonsignificant without specifying a test. Full-benchmark uncertainty reporting remains absent.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for the new analyses: at ten agents, Table 4 reports 55.2% for full MonoScale, 40.0% without negative memory, and 48.5% without customized warm-up; the new 20-agent HLE configuration reaches 23.4%. Table 2 changes the reported three-agent HLE accuracy from 11.60% to 11.70%. Core GAIA scores remain unchanged, and newly tabulated naive-scale-up overall scores already appeared in v1's Figure 1.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, assumptions, equations, and proofs are retained from v1's Appendix B in v2's Appendix C. Theorem 4.3 now explicitly names the existing non-interference and fallback assumptions, while Remark 4.4 explains their scope; neither introduces new mathematical substance.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution statement, and conclusion now explicitly condition the monotonicity guarantee on non-interfering expansion. This qualifies the prominent claim using assumptions already present in v1's technical material. The central contribution of stable expansion through familiarization and routing memory remains.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning negative routing constraints, transferable agent knowledge, and amortized onboarding cost. It introduces substantive limitations involving environment drift, memory saturation, long expansion horizons, and budget-induced over-decomposition, and acknowledges the local scaling dip. Section 6 also adds a rationale for comparing against fixed three-agent strong-router configurations.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code-access link, explicitly describes one-shot selection over finite memory candidates, and reports approximately $19.5 and 10–15 minutes per agent for onboarding. The detailed agent prompts and memory schemas are retained, as are the approximately 50 warm-up tasks and four rollouts per task.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning against UniRoute, StageRoute, and EvoRoute, distinguishing multi-step agent orchestration and reliability from model routing and cost–latency optimization. Fourteen cited works are added, extending coverage of agent risks, reusable skills, memory learning, and task synthesis.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized rewrites to related work, theoretical exposition, results, and discussion, renames Section 6 to Discussion and Limitations, and inserts a procedural appendix. The main narrative order and extensive prompt, schema, proof, and case-study text remain largely intact.

P2.justification: Tables 1 and 3 gain separate matched no-memory and memory blocks; v2 adds ablation and transfer tables plus Algorithm 1. Several figures move, including Figure 1 from the first to the second page. Existing plots, illustration content, and case-study table designs are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support for the central mechanism through controlled ablations that were absent from v1, supplemented by transfer and assumption checks. Explicit qualifications of the guarantee and analysis of the previously overlooked scaling dip improve scientific clarity. The small variance audit and overconfident predictability language in Section 6 remain weaknesses, but the stronger evidence and clearer applicability limits provide a substantial net improvement.
